newsitem.title: INDIA: India needs to relax import tariffs - policymaker.
newsitem.headline: India needs to relax import tariffs - policymaker.

text.p: A leading Indian policymaker said on Wednesday the country could face punitive action if it did not relax import restrictions as demanded by other member countries of the World Trade Organisation (WTO).

"We are on a weak wicket and we don't have any other option but to amend our laws," G.V. Ramakrishna, chairman of the government-appointed Disinvestment Commission told a seminar of the Associated Chambers of Commerce and Industry (ASSOCHAM).

"If the WTO rules against India, which it is most likely to, then there could be systematic punitive action ranging from import restrictions to tariff hikes and other such measures," Ramakrishna said.
He said India stood accused in complaints filed in the WTO by the United States, Japan, the European Union and some other countries, including Australia and Canada.
The major trade powers are protesting against India's decades-old import restrictions. They argue the Indian measures run against WTO open trading accords.

Last week Commerce Minister B.B. Ramaiah said India was confident of resolving the issue amicably. He said India had already reduced the timeframe for removing quantitative restrictions on imports to six years from an earlier proposal for nine years, and would stick to the six-year period.

The restrictions, which affect some 2,700 items ranging from consumer goods to agricultural products, have been in force since the 1950s, but were accepted by other countries because of India's earlier endemic balance-of-payments problems.
But with the steady growth in the country's foreign exchange reserves, which reached $28.8 billion in June, other WTO members have insisted Delhi agree to move quickly to drop the curbs.

The United States was reportedly pressing for a maximum of three years for a phase-out of restrictions, while the EU and other WTO members were indicating readiness to accept five years if limits on most big-ticket items were removed early in the period.
Under the WTO's dispute settlement procedure, India has to respond to the requests for consultations within 10 days and start them within 20 days.
If after two months no solution is in sight, the complaining powers can ask the WTO's Dispute Settlement Body to set up a panel to rule on the issue.
Ramakrishna also urged the government to take industry into its confidence on the agreements it enters into so that industry can brace itself for the challenges of open trade.
ASSOCHAM President H.L. Somany said Indian industry would have to gear itself to raise its efficiency to compete in domestic and international markets.
"Technology upgrades, emphasis on quality rather than quantity, will help us survive and flourish," Somany said.
